candidates.text: As a state may, for the purpose of guarding the morals of its own people, forbid all sales of lottery tickets within its limits
candidates.speaker: Harlan
candidates.reason: States the rule that the power to regulate commerce includes the power to prohibit it. Count excluded: 'widespread pestilence' is quoted from Phalen v. Virginia (1850), predating the case.

candidates.text: We are of opinion that lottery tickets are subjects of traffic, and therefore are subjects of commerce
candidates.speaker: Harlan
phrases: lottery tickets are subjects of traffic, and therefore are subjects of commerce
candidates.reason: States the first holding: lottery tickets are articles of commerce.

candidates.text: If a state, when considering legislation for the suppression of lotteries within its own limits, may properly take into view the evils
candidates.speaker: Harlan
phrases: shall not be polluted by the carrying of lottery tickets from one state to another
candidates.reason: The 'pollution' passage the Critique treats as central.

candidates.text: An invitation to dine, or to take a drive, or a note of introduction, all become articles of commerce
candidates.speaker: Fuller
phrases: An invitation to dine, or to take a drive, or a note of introduction

candidates.text: But, as often said, the possible abuse of a power is not an argument against its existence
candidates.speaker: Harlan
